title: Conditionals
note: One file for the whole topic: the rules page, the practice page and the quiz all read this. `rules` and `gapfill.tests` share their ids (zero, first, …), which is how a wrong answer shows the form that governs it. `structure` and `explanation` were added to each rules section for that purpose — the sections previously carried only worked examples.

rules.title: ZERO
rules.subtitle: General truths & facts

examples.before: If you <<heat>> water to 100°C, it <<boils>>.
examples.after: Water <<boils>> if you <<heat>> it to 100°C.

examples.before: If you <<mix>> red and blue, you <<get>> purple.
examples.after: You <<get>> purple if you <<mix>> red and blue.

examples.before: If plants <<don't get>> water, they <<die>>.
examples.after: Plants <<die>> if they <<don't get>> water.

examples.before: If you <<press>> this button, the machine <<stops>>.
examples.after: The machine <<stops>> if you <<press>> this button.

examples.before: If ice <<melts>>, it <<becomes>> water.
examples.after: Ice <<becomes>> water if it <<melts>>.

examples.before: If I <<wake up>> late, I <<miss>> the bus.
examples.after: I <<miss>> the bus if I <<wake up>> late.

examples.before: If she <<drinks>> coffee at night, she <<can't sleep>>.
examples.after: She <<can't sleep>> if she <<drinks>> coffee at night.

examples.before: If it <<rains>>, we <<take>> the car.
examples.after: We <<take>> the car if it <<rains>>.

examples.before: If he <<feels>> stressed, he <<goes>> for a run.
examples.after: He <<goes>> for a run if he <<feels>> stressed.

examples.before: If you <<heat>> metal, it <<expands>>.
examples.after: Metal <<expands>> if you <<heat>> it.

rules.explanation: Use the zero conditional for general truths, scientific facts and things that always happen under the same conditions. Both halves are present simple, and 'if' can be replaced by 'when' without changing the meaning.

rules.title: FIRST
rules.subtitle: Real future possibilities

examples.before: If it <<rains>> tomorrow, we <<will cancel>> the picnic.
examples.after: We <<will cancel>> the picnic if it <<rains>> tomorrow.

examples.before: If you <<study>> hard, you <<will pass>> the exam.
examples.after: You <<will pass>> the exam if you <<study>> hard.

examples.before: If she <<arrives>> early, I <<will meet>> her at the station.
examples.after: I <<will meet>> her at the station if she <<arrives>> early.

examples.before: If they <<don't hurry>>, they <<will miss>> the train.
examples.after: They <<will miss>> the train if they <<don't hurry>>.

examples.before: If we <<leave>> now, we <<will arrive>> on time.
examples.after: We <<will arrive>> on time if we <<leave>> now.

examples.before: If you <<need>> help, I <<will call>> you.
examples.after: I <<will call>> you if you <<need>> help.

examples.before: If you <<don't wear>> a coat, you <<will get>> cold.
examples.after: You <<will get>> cold if you <<don't wear>> a coat.

examples.before: If she <<finishes>> early, she <<will help>> us.
examples.after: She <<will help>> us if she <<finishes>> early.

examples.before: If the weather <<improves>>, we <<will go>> to the beach.
examples.after: We <<will go>> to the beach if the weather <<improves>>.

examples.before: If you <<touch>> that wire, you <<will get>> an electric shock.
examples.after: You <<will get>> an electric shock if you <<touch>> that wire.

examples.before: If you <<see>> John, <<tell>> him to call me.
examples.after: <<Tell>> John to call me if you <<see>> him.

examples.before: If the phone <<rings>>, <<answer>> it please.
examples.after: <<Answer>> the phone if it <<rings>>, please.

examples.before: If you <<finish>> early, <<send>> me an email.
examples.after: <<Send>> me an email if you <<finish>> early.

examples.before: If anyone <<asks>>, <<say>> I'm in a meeting.
examples.after: <<Say>> I'm in a meeting if anyone <<asks>>.

examples.before: If it <<gets>> too hot, <<open>> the window.
examples.after: <<Open>> the window if it <<gets>> too hot.

rules.explanation: Use the first conditional for a real, likely possibility in the future. The if-clause stays in the present simple even though it refers to the future — 'if it will rain' is the classic error. The result clause takes 'will', or an imperative for instructions.

rules.title: SECOND
rules.subtitle: Unreal present situations

examples.before: If I <<were>> rich, I <<would travel>> around the world.
examples.after: I <<would travel>> around the world if I <<were>> rich.

examples.before: If she <<had>> more time, she <<would learn>> a new language.
examples.after: She <<would learn>> a new language if she <<had>> more time.

examples.before: If we <<lived>> closer, we <<would visit>> you more often.
examples.after: We <<would visit>> you more often if we <<lived>> closer.

examples.before: If he <<knew>> the answer, he <<would tell>> us.
examples.after: He <<would tell>> us if he <<knew>> the answer.

examples.before: If you <<studied>> harder, you <<would get>> better grades.
examples.after: You <<would get>> better grades if you <<studied>> harder.

examples.before: If I <<were>> you, I <<would accept>> the job offer.
examples.after: I <<would accept>> the job offer if I <<were>> you.

examples.before: If you <<asked>> him nicely, he <<would probably help>>.
examples.after: He <<would probably help>> if you <<asked>> him nicely.

examples.before: If she <<took>> a taxi, she <<would arrive>> faster.
examples.after: She <<would arrive>> faster if she <<took>> a taxi.

examples.before: If they <<practiced>> more, they <<would improve>> quickly.
examples.after: They <<would improve>> quickly if they <<practiced>> more.

examples.before: If we <<started>> earlier, we <<wouldn't be>> so rushed.
examples.after: We <<wouldn't be>> so rushed if we <<started>> earlier.

examples.before: If I <<could fly>>, I <<would visit>> every country.
examples.after: I <<would visit>> every country if I <<could fly>>.

examples.before: If dogs <<could talk>>, they <<would tell>> us their secrets.
examples.after: Dogs <<would tell>> us their secrets if they <<could talk>>.

examples.before: If she <<won>> the lottery, she <<would buy>> a mansion.
examples.after: She <<would buy>> a mansion if she <<won>> the lottery.

examples.before: If time travel <<were>> possible, I <<would visit>> the past.
examples.after: I <<would visit>> the past if time travel <<were>> possible.

examples.before: If he <<weren't>> so shy, he <<would make>> more friends.
examples.after: He <<would make>> more friends if he <<weren't>> so shy.

rules.explanation: Use the second conditional for situations that are hypothetical, unlikely or contrary to the present facts. The past simple here does not refer to past time — it signals distance from reality. 'Were' is used for all persons in careful writing: 'if I were you'.

rules.title: THIRD
rules.subtitle: Unreal past situations

examples.before: If I <<had known>>, I <<would have helped>> you.
examples.after: I <<would have helped>> you if I <<had known>>.

examples.before: If she <<had studied>> harder, she <<would have passed>> the exam.
examples.after: She <<would have passed>> the exam if she <<had studied>> harder.

examples.before: If they <<had left>> earlier, they <<wouldn't have missed>> the train.
examples.after: They <<wouldn't have missed>> the train if they <<had left>> earlier.

examples.before: If we <<had taken>> a map, we <<wouldn't have got>> lost.
examples.after: We <<wouldn't have got>> lost if we <<had taken>> a map.

examples.before: If he <<had been>> more careful, the accident <<wouldn't have happened>>.
examples.after: The accident <<wouldn't have happened>> if he <<had been>> more careful.

examples.before: If you <<had told>> me, I <<would have understood>>.
examples.after: I <<would have understood>> if you <<had told>> me.

examples.before: If it <<had rained>>, the match <<would have been>> cancelled.
examples.after: The match <<would have been>> cancelled if it <<had rained>>.

examples.before: If she <<had accepted>> the offer, she <<would be>> rich now.
examples.after: She <<would be>> rich now if she <<had accepted>> the offer.

examples.before: If they <<had invited>> us, we <<would have gone>>.
examples.after: We <<would have gone>> if they <<had invited>> us.

examples.before: If I <<had seen>> the sign, I <<would have stopped>>.
examples.after: I <<would have stopped>> if I <<had seen>> the sign.

rules.structure: if + past perfect, would have + past participle
rules.explanation: Use the third conditional for an unreal past: something that did not happen, and its imagined result. Both halves look backwards, and nothing can now change the outcome, which is why it so often carries regret or criticism.

examples.after: She <<would have fixed>> it herself if she <<knew>> about computers.

examples.after: We <<would have>> food ready now if we <<had known>> you were coming.

examples.before: If he <<spoke>> French, he <<could have got>> that job in Paris.
examples.after: He <<could have got>> that job in Paris if he <<spoke>> French.

examples.before: If they <<had invested>> wisely, they <<would be enjoying>> retirement now.
examples.after: They <<would be enjoying>> retirement now if they <<had invested>> wisely.

examples.before: If I <<had saved>> more money, I <<would have>> a car now.
examples.after: I <<would have>> a car now if I <<had saved>> more money.

examples.before: If she <<had gone>> to university, she <<would be>> a doctor today.
examples.after: She <<would be>> a doctor today if she <<had gone>> to university.

examples.before: If we <<had bought>> that house, we <<would still be>> living there.
examples.after: We <<would still be>> living there if we <<had bought>> that house.

examples.before: If he <<had learned>> to drive, he <<wouldn't need>> a taxi now.

examples.before: If they <<had invested>> in that company, they <<would be>> millionaires.
examples.after: They <<would be>> millionaires if they <<had invested>> in that company.

rules.structure: if + past perfect, would + infinitive  /  if + past simple, would have + past participle
rules.explanation: Use a mixed conditional when the time of the condition and the time of the result differ. Most often a past condition with a present result ('if I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now'), but the reverse also occurs. The time words in the sentence — 'now', 'yesterday' — tell you which half belongs to which time.
